nameStory: This tiny copepod doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists stick with its formal Latin name Aglaodiaptomus spatulocrenatus. The genus name 'Aglaodiaptomus' means 'bright swimmer' in Greek, referring to these microscopic creatures' graceful movement through the water. The species name 'spatulocrenatus' describes the spoon-like shape of certain body parts that help identify this particular species.
description: This is a microscopic freshwater copepod - a tiny crustacean that swims freely in ponds and lakes. At less than 2 millimeters long, it's about the size of a large grain of sand and would be nearly impossible to see without magnification. Like other copepods, it has a teardrop-shaped body with long antennae that it uses like oars to propel itself through the water in jerky, hopping movements. This species belongs to a group of copepods that are important food for fish and other aquatic animals.

idTips.label: Body size and shape
idTips.description: Extremely small at 1-2mm long with a characteristic teardrop or pear-shaped body that tapers toward the tail

idTips.label: Swimming pattern
idTips.description: Moves through water with distinctive jerky, hopping motions rather than smooth gliding

idTips.label: Antenna length
idTips.description: First pair of antennae (antennules) are very long, often extending well beyond the body length

idTips.label: Specialized appendages
idTips.description: Males have modified right antenna that forms a grasping structure; females have distinctive spoon-shaped structures on reproductive segments

idTips.label: Body segmentation
idTips.description: Clear division between front body section (prosome) and narrower tail section (urosome)

habitat: Found in freshwater lakes and larger ponds throughout New England, typically in the open water column rather than near shores. Prefers cooler, deeper waters and is most common in oligotrophic lakes - those that are clear and low in nutrients. Often found alongside other planktonic organisms in the same water column.

seasonality.spring: Populations begin to increase as water warms, with reproduction ramping up. Best time to find adults in breeding condition.
seasonality.summer: Peak abundance in cooler, deeper lake waters. May be less active during warmest periods and retreat to deeper, cooler layers.
seasonality.fall: Still active but populations may decline. Some individuals may be producing resting eggs to survive winter.
seasonality.winter: Present but less active in ice-covered waters, often in deeper layers where temperatures are more stable.

funFact: Despite being nearly invisible to the naked eye, these tiny copepods can live for several months and are such efficient swimmers that they can cover distances equivalent to a human swimming several miles - all while being smaller than the period at the end of this sentence!
confusionNotes: Extremely difficult to distinguish from other copepod species without microscopic examination of specialized appendages. The spoon-shaped reproductive structures are the key identifying feature, but require significant magnification to observe clearly.
contextualKnowledge: This species is so rarely observed (only 2 recorded sightings in New England) that it may be genuinely rare in the region, or simply overlooked due to the specialized equipment and expertise needed to identify microscopic freshwater plankton. Most people encounter copepods as a group rather than identifying individual species.
compareHints: **Note: Identification uncertain due to limited reference material** This appears to be the only Aglaodiaptomus species commonly found in New England waters. It differs from other calanoid copepods in the region by its specific combination of body proportions and the distinctive spoon-shaped structures on reproductive segments. Other diaptomid copepods in New England waters typically belong to different genera with different appendage structures and body shapes.
